The Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 was moved to require active consent from class action members, cap funder and lawyer shares at 30% of proceeds, and mandate court approval of distributions to ensure fair returns for claimants, citing cases like Banksia Securities and Wittenbury v Vocation where funders and lawyers took nearly 50% of settlements.

The speaker argued the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 is Orwellian and will harm ordinary Australians' access to justice, citing a 30 per cent cap on costs and a switch to opt-in class actions as design features that benefit defendants. He announced Labor will oppose the bill and move a second reading amendment, referencing the robodebt scheme (430,000 victims, $1.7 billion restitution) and an underpaid Aboriginal wages case as examples of class actions that would be prevented.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 is needed to regulate litigation funders and ensure class action members receive at least 70% of claim proceeds, with a rebuttable presumption against non-member distributions exceeding 30%. The bill responds to Australian Law Reform Commission findings showing median plaintiff returns drop from 85% (without funders) to 51% (with funders), and to a parliamentary committee’s 31 recommendations.

The Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 would restrict access to class actions for many Australians, particularly victims of financial fraud like those from the Trio Capital collapse, by imposing court approval requirements and a rebuttable presumption that distributions under 70% to plaintiffs are unfair. The bill was criticised for its rushed inquiry process, which gave the public only days to respond, and for potentially discouraging settlements, increasing costs, and benefiting wealthy defendants over ordinary plaintiffs.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 addresses the free rider problem in open class actions by establishing a new managed investment scheme for litigation funding and requiring fair and reasonable returns to funders, based on recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Corporations and Financial Services and the Australian Law Reform Commission.

The speaker opposed the Corporations Amendment Bill, arguing that class actions are the only means of redress for people harmed by government and corporate actions—citing Queensland taxi owners, stolen wages for Indigenous Australians, and the live cattle export ban—and warned of personal retaliation against those who destroy livelihoods.

The speech supported the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing that litigation funders exploit vulnerable plaintiffs by taking large shares of court-awarded compensation. It argued for stronger regulation and court oversight of litigation funding contracts while affirming that class actions remain legal.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 is a deceptive attempt by the Morrison-Joyce government to protect wealthy defendants by making class actions harder for everyday Australians, contrary to its stated consumer protection purpose. They cited opposition from the Law Council, Phi Finney McDonald, and defendant lawyers at Herbert Smith Freehills, and noted constitutional concerns raised by Justice Beach and former Solicitor-General Justin Gleeson SC, as well as specific class actions—including stolen wages, stolen generations, Westpac overcharging, PFAS contamination, and Domino’s underpayment cases—that would not have proceeded under the bill.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment Bill 2021 would harm access to justice by making class actions harder, citing that community legal centres turn away over 160,000 people annually and that the bill would have required 430,000 robodebt class action members to opt in. The speaker announced Labor's opposition to the bill.

The speaker opposed the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing it would restrict class actions by requiring court approval for funding agreements over 30% and shifting from an opt-out to an opt-in system, thereby making it harder for ordinary Australians, particularly remote and Indigenous communities, to access justice.

The speaker argued the bill is misleadingly titled and will actually hinder access to justice by protecting wealthy defendants, citing constitutional concerns, a rushed and inadequate consultation process, and examples of landmark class actions—such as stolen wages and environmental contamination cases—that would be blocked under its measures.

The speaker opposed the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing it would harm access to justice by making class actions harder to bring. They cited examples such as a $500 million settlement for 2009 Victorian bushfire survivors, a $112 million robodebt class action for 450,000 people, and actions against major banks and Sigma Pharmaceuticals, and noted concerns from legal expert Justin Gleeson that the bill may be unconstitutional.

The speaker opposed the 30% cap on litigation funder fees in the Corporations Amendment Bill, arguing it would reduce access to justice for small businesses and individuals by altering funders' risk-reward calculations. He cited high legal costs, a defamation case costing nearly $2 million without trial, and discrepancies between TGA and AusVaxSafety data on COVID vaccine adverse events.

The speaker opposed the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing it would replace the opt-out class action model with an opt-in requirement and flawed fund distribution rules, making class actions harder for ordinary Australians while protecting large corporations. They urged the government to withdraw or vote against the bill.

The speaker supported the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing it would ensure class action claimants receive a fairer share of damages by capping litigation funders’ take at 30% and citing cases where claimants received as little as 33% of settlements.

The speaker argued the bill makes justice harder for ordinary Australians, citing expert John Sheahan's view that it "makes things worse for everyone." They opposed the 70-30 cost split and opt-in requirement, claiming these will block meritorious claims and protect large corporate defendants, while criticizing the rushed three-week committee process and lack of a proper regulatory impact statement.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 would fundamentally weaken class actions by shifting from an opt-out to an opt-in structure, denying access to justice for vulnerable people, especially in rural, regional and remote communities. They also criticised the bill's process as atrocious and biased, and claimed it was possibly unconstitutional and driven by ideology rather than evidence.

The Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 lowers the registration threshold for political campaigners from $500,000 to $100,000 in electoral expenditure, and introduces a new requirement to register if spending at least $14,500 and one-third of revenue. The bill implements recommendation 18 of the JSCEM report on the 2019 federal election to align transparency rules for political actors with those for parties and candidates.

Labor opposed the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021, arguing it would lower the political campaigner threshold for charities and not-for-profits from $500,000 or two-thirds of annual income to $100,000 or one-third, imposing heavy disclosure requirements and foreign-donation bans that silence critics. The speaker moved a second reading amendment calling for the donation disclosure threshold to be reduced from $14,500 to a fixed $1,000 with real-time disclosure, and criticised the Morrison government for failing to deliver a national anti-corruption commission and for pursuing voter ID laws.

The speaker argued the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 would enhance transparency by requiring organisations spending over $100,000 or $14,500 (if over a third of annual revenue) on electoral expenditure to register as political campaigners, implementing recommendation 18 of the 2019 election inquiry.
